records.text: 70. The Special Rapporteur recommends that the Government: (a) Strengthen the commitment to combat the sale, sexual exploitation and sexual abuse of children with sustainable resources, especially for service providers so that they can provide the necessary care and support for child victims and survivors; (b) Ensure that all relevant stakeholders adopt interdisciplinary and child ‐ centred approaches when providing care and support to child victims; (c) Ensure adequate resources and training for youth welfare offices across the country to make their services available to all children everywhere in Germany, especially those in vulnerable situations; (d) Encourage the establishment of a childhood house in every federal state in Germany; (e) Ground the childhood houses in law to ensure their sustainability and authority in child protection; (f) Establish specialized counselling centres for child victims of trafficking across the country, with a view to having at least one centre in every federal state, including by expanding the mandate of existing counselling centres for adults to provide services for children; (g) Equip specialized counselling centres with the required competencies and resources to provide child-centred services for child victims of trafficking in line with their needs and best interests ; (h) Provide strengthened support and adequate resources to civil society initiatives that provide care and support to child victims of abuse or exploitation, including boys and children with other gender identities; (i) Ensure the availability of specialized shelters that meet the standard of appropriate and safe accommodation for all genders and age groups in all federal states.

records.section: Prevention and eradication of the sale, sexual exploitation and sexual abuse of children
records.text: 68. The Special Rapporteur recommends that the Government: (a) Incorporate age-appropriate sexuality education and digital literacy, including on the prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse in both the online and offline environments, as a compulsory subject for all children in all schools across the country; (b) Encourage and support creative initiatives to raise the awareness of children on their rights, on how to recognize sexual exploitation and abuse and on where to find help and support; (c) Equip teachers with the ability and training to teach sexuality education and digital literacy, including on the prevention of child sexual exploitation and abuse in both the online and offline environments, through pre-service and regular in-service training; (d) Provide adequate resources for schools to develop and implement child protection strategies; (e) Include child protection in the curricula of social work studies to ensure that youth welfare office employees have the necessary capacity to work on child protection; (f) Provide mandatory training on children’s rights and protection, including from child sexual abuse and exploitation, for professionals who work or come in contact with children, including educators, health and legal professionals, law enforcement officials, judicial and court officials and employees and volunteers in areas relating to sports, culture and leisure activities; (g) Mandate all institutions and organizations working for and with children to develop and implement comprehensive child safeguarding policies that include child protection measures in the digital space, as relevant; (h) Collaborate with religious institutions to strengthen their accountability and transparency procedures in child sexual abuse cases; (i) Strengthen initiatives to raise public awareness on child protection risks in the digital environment, including the risks associated with posting photos and videos of children online; (j) Ensure a standardized approach for and the coordination of awareness ‐ raising activities across the country among child protection actors; (k) Mandate digital service providers to implement strong due diligence measures and ensure that the rights and best interests of children are key considerations when designing their services; (l) Mandate transparency from digital service providers concerning their use of artificial intelligence and algorithms and their implementation of risk analysis and risk mitigating measures; (m) Encourage commercial travel providers to subscribe to the Code of Conduct for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation in Travel and Tourism; (n) Strengthen public information campaigns on child sexual abuse and exploitation in strategic areas, including airports and train and bus stations; (o) Include information on voluntourism in travel advisories and raise awareness of the risks, particularly for countries with a high risk of child sexual exploitation; (p) Address the root causes of the sexual exploitation of children in vulnerable situations, including refugee and migrant children, in cooperation, where appropriate, with the countries of origin of the children.

The Special Rapporteur recommends that the Government: (a) Adopt a national child protection strategy with an oversight mechanism to ensure consistency and harmony in approaches and implementation across the country; (b) Appoint a national commissioner for children’s rights to, inter alia, ensure that laws and practices relating to children conform with the minimum requirements provided for under the Convention on the Rights of the Child; (c) Evaluate the Action Plan for the Protection of Children and Young People from Sexual Violence and Exploitation to track progress and identify gaps; (d) Provide a permanent legislative basis for the National Rapporteur Mechanism on trafficking in persons; (e) Ensure the implementation of the new National Action Plan to Prevent and Combat Trafficking in Human Beings and Protect Trafficked Persons in all federal states, with a specific focus on child protection and child-centred approaches; (f) Establish a central coordination office on trafficking in persons at the federal state level; (g) Harmonize the legal framework for public and commercial services dealing with children to ensure the same child protection standards for all activities relating to children both in Germany and abroad; (h) Develop a national action plan on combating online child sexual abuse and exploitation; (i) Update and ensure the adequacy of the legal framework to ensure its responsiveness to the evolving nature of online child sexual exploitation and abuse offences; (j) Replace all references in the law to “ child pornography ” with “ child sexual abuse material ” , in line with the Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse ; (k) Support the proposal to recast Directive 2011/93/EU on combating the sexual abuse and sexual exploitation of children and child pornography.

records.text: 61. Germany has been devoting increased attention and resources to improving its policy, legal and institutional frameworks for the prevention of the sale, sexual abuse and exploitation of children and their protection from such offences . Over the years, robust legal frameworks and structures have been put in place to respond to the different manifestations of the phenomena. 62. The federal nature of the governance structure , together with the high number of child protection actors across the country , may pose a challenge to the effective coordination of procedures and practices in responding to incidences of child sexual abuse and exploitation. Each of the federal states and municipalities in Germany adopts varying approaches and practices on child protection. While that allows for tailoring to local needs and contexts, it often results in fragmented measures and a lack of coordinat ion , which in turn affect the care and services provided to children. There is a need to ensure consistency and harmony in approaches and implementation across the country. A child anywhere in Germany should receive equal protection of their rights and similar support services and care. 63. All efforts towards combating child sexual exploitation and abuse must take into account the specific situation and needs of children, particularly those in vulnerable situations, such as children with disabilities, refugee and asylum-seeking children and migrant children. Children are rights holders with their own agency. There is a need to shift the focus from the right of parents to protect children to the right of children , as individual rights holders , to be protected. To th at end, children should be at the centre of every initiative and decision relating to the provision of care and services to them and should be able to meaningfully participate in decision-making processes that affect them. 64. The apparent conflict between data protection and child protection is a recurring theme in the country. Child protection actors often fear violating data protection laws if they exchange information on children in need of care and protection, inhibiting the identification of victims and the provision of appropriate care and support. That concern is caused by a lack of understanding on the part of child protection professionals as to how data protection laws are applicable in relation to their roles. The protection and best interests of the child should be the paramount consideration of any person or authority dealing with a child protection issue. 65. Sustainable and consistent intersectoral collaboration among all child protection actors at the national, federal state and municipal levels is key to effectively combating and preventing the sale, sexual abuse and sexual exploitation of children. The strong commitment from the Government to addressing the issues of the sale, sexual exploitation and sexual abuse of children and providing victims with the requisite care and support must be accompanied by sustainable resources, especially for relevant service providers so that they can provide the necessary care and support for child victims and survivors.

records.text: Data 59. Local child and youth welfare authorities are obliged to collect data on child endangerment cases on an ongoing basis, disaggregated by type of endangerment and perpetrator, risk assessment, gender, age, assistance, place of residence and parents’ nationality, among other categories, and to transmit the data to the statistical offices of the federal state, which then transmit them to the Federal Statistical Office. The Federal Criminal Police Office also compiles crime statistics on the basis of data provided by the criminal investigation offices in the 16 federal states. The federal report on sexual offences against children and young people has been available since 2022. The data are aggregated by, inter alia, type of offences and the age and sex of victims and perpetrators. In the context of trafficking in persons, following the establishment of the National Rapporteur Mechanism on trafficking in persons, the federal report brings together, in one publication, the available data from federal and federal state authorities, specialized counselling centres and civil society organizations, such as the Bundesweiter Koordinierungskreis gegen Menschenhandel. 60. The Special Rapporteur appreciates the efforts that the Government has made in data collection and encourages the strengthening and harmonization of the data collection processes within the federal Government and the federal states and among local authorities and civil society organizations to ensure comprehensive, systematically collected, reliable and disaggregated data on the sexual abuse and exploitation of children and its different manifestations, with an emphasis on children in vulnerable situations.

records.text: 56. It was also brought to the Special Rapporteur’s attention that, while video hearings of children were legally possible, they were subject to certain practical hurdles. Depending on the equipment and the procedure, video interviews are carried out more often in some federal states than others. In addition, the courts do not consistently accept video recordings to replace children’s direct statements at trial, pointing to a lack of knowledge of child-friendly procedures. The Special Rapporteur notes with appreciation that, in 2021, the National Council against Sexual Violence Committed against Children and Young People published a practical guide on the application of child-friendly criteria for criminal proceedings. Developed for police officers, public prosecutors and judges, the guide was the result of consultations and discussions with judges, public prosecutors, the police, lawyers, the Survivors’ Board, counselling centres, victim support institutions, child protection organizations and academia. In 2022, the National Council published a practical guide on the application of child-friendly criteria for family court proceedings aimed primarily at family law judges and other actors in family court proceedings, including youth welfare office employees, guardians ad litem and lawyers. The Special Rapporteur encourages the Government to provide additional and regular training for prosecutors and judges to ensure that they are able to implement child-friendly procedures.

records.text: 54. The Federal Criminal Police Office is well positioned for the fight against child sexual exploitation and abuse online and well connected internationally. Investigative authorities at the federal state level are also equipped to combat such phenomena and have managed to uncover and stop ongoing abuse and exploitation. Nevertheless, due to the constantly evolving avenues for the rapid dissemination of content on the Internet and the continuous increase in storage capacity via data carriers and cloud services, law enforcement agencies are increasingly confronted with challenges in investigating cases. The use of end-to-end encrypted platforms to exchange child sexual abuse material and to communicate without detection has further complicated the work of investigators. In addition, the sheer amount of child sexual abuse material and the number of reports can overwhelm the available resources. 55. The Special Rapporteur was pleased to learn that, within the judiciary, family court judges were required to have proven knowledge of the laws on parent and child matters, of the available child and youth welfare services and of child developmental psychology and communication with children, or must acquire such knowledge as soon as possible. Nevertheless, continuous training for criminal and family court judges on children’s rights, child protection and, specifically, child sexual abuse and exploitation is needed.

Furthermore, there is a need for more capacity-building for law enforcement personnel to strengthen their skills in the detection of crimes and the identification of victims of trafficking in children and to equip them with the tools that they need to meet their evidential burden during criminal proceedings against alleged perpetrators. In Germany, there are many national organizations specializing in issues of trafficking in persons, such as the Bundesweiter Koordinierungskreis gegen Menschenhandel (National Coordination Group against Trafficking in Persons) and ECPAT Germany, which offer extensive capacity-building opportunities to law enforcement agencies. The Special Rapporteur commends their work and urges the Government to support such organizations with sufficient funding and resources.

records.section: Investigation, prosecution and access to justice
records.text: 52. Discussions revealed that the challenges in investigating cases of trafficking in persons in Germany included a lack of clarity on the relevant provision within the Criminal Code and a lack of knowledge on the part of the investigative authorities and the judiciary on how to interpret the provision. The titles of the provisions in the Criminal Code can create confusion around the applicable legal provision on child trafficking offences. Section 236 of the Criminal Code, entitled “Child Trafficking”, actually regulates offences relating to the sale of children. Meanwhile, section 232, entitled “Human Trafficking”, and section 233, entitled “Exploitation of Labour”, regulate all the relevant trafficking in persons offences, including trafficking in children. In addition, due to the complexity and high evidential requirements, investigations into trafficking in children sometimes fall back on the offence of child sexual abuse or of inducing children to engage in sexual activity. Failing to distinguish linguistically between the offence of child sexual abuse and trafficking in children may lead to inadequate care, support and protection.

records.text: 48. The Special Rapporteur visited the childhood houses in Berlin and Düsseldorf, which are outpatient, child-friendly, multidisciplinary points of contact and support for children and young people affected by violence. The childhood houses offer a place for child victims to be examined and interviewed in a safe and child-friendly environment by professionals. She observed that all of the professions involved – medical and psychological and the youth welfare and criminal justice systems – worked together under one roof in a coordinated and collaborative manner to reduce the possibility of retraumatizing the child. Currently, there are 11 childhood houses in Germany. The Special Rapporteur commends the childhood house initiative and urges its replication in every federal state. She also encourages the Government to ground the childhood houses in law to ensure their sustainability and their authority in child protection. 49. The Special Rapporteur wishes to showcase the Hilfe-für-Jungs “Subway” project, financed by the Berlin Senate Department for Education, Youth and Family, which is aimed at providing care and support to boys, young men and non-binary persons affected by sexual abuse and exploitation. She visited the organization’s premises and participated in its nighttime street outreach activities to learn about the realities and struggles faced by its clients. The organization provides various services, including shelter, food, medical care, psychosocial counselling, legal advice and sexuality education, including information on sexual and reproductive health and rights. Hilfe-für-Jungs works closely with the relevant authorities, primarily the local youth welfare office, to ensure the protection and well-being of child victims. As of October 2024, the organization had directed 11 child protection reports to the youth welfare office on boys suspected of being victims of sexual exploitation. To allow for sustained efforts in the care and support of boys and children of other gender identities, the Special Rapporteur calls for continued support and the allocation of adequate resources to such initiatives. 50. Specialist counselling centres play an important role in Germany in police work and in identifying and supporting victims of trafficking in persons. They provide various services, including counselling, psychological care and support to victims before, during and after interviews with the police and court appearances, thereby contributing significantly to the success of criminal proceedings. With regard to shelters, only eight federal states have shelters that cater specifically to the needs of victims of trafficking in persons. There are no facilities specialized in the accommodation of child or adolescent victims. The Special Rapporteur recommends that the Government ensure the availability of specialized shelters that meet the standard of appropriate and safe accom­modation for all genders and age groups in all federal states. 51. Victims of sexual exploitation and abuse in Germany are entitled to rapid assistance in the form of psychosocial and outpatient trauma counselling. A prerequisite for receiving outpatient trauma counselling is for victims to seek counselling within 12 months of experiencing the harmful event. Should the offence have occurred more than 12 months earlier, those affected can claim services if the offence led to an acute crisis. That is particularly relevant for people who were victims of sexual violence during their childhood and who, years later, experience a trigger that causes an acute crisis.

records.text: 41. In Germany, professionals who work with children, including medical personnel, psychologists, social workers and teachers, are usually bound by professional confidentiality regulations. Nevertheless, if they suspect child endangerment, they must discuss the situation with the child and with the legal guardian, where appropriate, and are entitled to seek the advice of a child protection specialist from a youth welfare agency. In doing so, they are allowed to share information with the specialist, albeit pseudonymized. The youth welfare office that receives information from any source on potential threats to a child must carry out a child risk assessment and may decide to provide assistance or involve other relevant stakeholders, such as the police or medical personnel, according to the needs of the child. In the event that a child faces imminent danger, the local youth welfare office is mandated to take the child into its care, which includes placing the child with a suitable person or institution or in another form of housing. 42. The Special Rapporteur’s discussions indicated that there was no clear understanding among child protection actors on how information exchange and data protection laws should be applied as they related to their roles as child protection professionals. The fear of violating data protection laws can inhibit the exchange of information, which is vital for identifying victims and ensuring appropriate care and support. It bears noting that, in Germany, child protection takes precedence over data protection and the law provides clear requirements on the sharing of data and information in cases of a suspected threat to the welfare of the child. More training is required for child protection actors and professionals on their mandate to ensure the uninhibited multi-stakeholder exchange of information regarding a child in need of care and protection. 43. The Special Rapporteur notes with appreciation that the law requires youth welfare offices to employ only those who have received training corresponding to their respective tasks. They must also ensure further training for their staff. She notes with regret, however, that the law does not specifically mandate child protection training, especially given its importance and relevance to the daily work of the youth welfare offices. It has been reported that the majority of professionals in youth welfare offices have social work qualifications and varying levels of knowledge and competencies in child protection. The Government is encouraged to include child protection in the curricula of social work studies. 44. The Special Rapporteur was pleased to learn that, in 2014, the Independent Federal Commissioner against Child Sexual Abuse had launched a helpline (0800 22 55 530) specifically for the anonymous reporting of child sexual abuse; it provides free, multilingual advice and sign-language support. People can contact the helpline if they are worried about a child, whether or not they are personally affected. There is also a helpline (116 111) for broader issues relating to children. That helpline is also free and enables anonymous reporting. Managed by Nummer gegen Kummer (Number against distress), the helpline provides an accessible consultation and counselling service for children, young people, parents and other caregivers across the country. It serves as the first point of contact for questions, problems and even critical situations. While the helplines are promising practices, the Special Rapporteur observes that children may face challenges in reporting abuse or exploitation, given the federal structure of the protection system. For example, some municipalities have their own helplines or other reporting channels. 45. Child sexual abuse material can be reported on various platforms, including the Freiwillige Selbstkontrolle Multimedia-Diensteanbieter (Voluntary self-regulation of multimedia service providers), the eco – Association of the Internet Industry and the Jugendschutz.net platforms. In 2024, the Freiwillige Selbstkontrolle Multimedia-Diensteanbieter platform received a total of 25,536 reports about material that was illegal or harmful for young people; 8,077 of the reported cases concerned child sexual abuse material. The same year, Jugendschutz.net received 17,630 reports, 90 per cent of which related to online child sexual exploitation and abuse. The Special Rapporteur expresses concern about the lack of obligation for the private sector to report child sexual abuse material, which she learned about during her visit. She also learned about the lack of regulations mandating transparency in the private sector around the use of artificial intelligence, algorithms, risk analysis and risk mitigating measures. She is concerned, for example, about reports that the algorithms used by some providers push violent or other harmful content towards children and young people. 46. The Special Rapporteur observes that Germany does not have a nationally standardized procedure for the identification of victims of trafficking. There is no national referral mechanism that coordinates cooperation among all relevant bodies, which means that victims of trafficking are left to the structures and services available wherever they find them. She also understands that only eight federal states provide shelters for adult victims of trafficking and that there are no shelters for child victims of trafficking. That situation points to the need to do more to protect child victims of trafficking in its different forms, including by establishing a systemic response to the trafficking of children. 47. The IN VIA Specialist Advisory and Coordination Centre for Trafficking in and Exploitation of Minors in Berlin, established in early 2024, is financed by the Berlin Senate Department for Education, Youth and Family. The Special Rapporteur attended the official launch during her visit. She learned that the centre was aimed at providing child-centred support by empowering all relevant actors on early detection and the identification of affected children and strengthening the collaboration between the youth welfare system, criminal investigatory agencies and institutions involved in victim protection. She commends the initiative and recommends the establishment of at least one such specialized counselling centre for child victims of trafficking in every federal state. Where necessary, the mandate of existing counselling centres for adults could be expanded to include the provision of services to children, provided that the centres are equipped with the required competencies and resources.

records.text: 34. Education serves as one of the most effective means of combating the sale, sexual exploitation and sexual abuse of children. The Special Rapporteur was pleased to learn that, in Germany, sexuality education is mandatory starting in primary school. Although education is within the purview of each federal state, the Federal Institute of Public Health (formerly Federal Centre for Health Education) produces the framework for sexuality education and a national curriculum in collaboration with the federal states, which provide the conceptual basis for sexuality education. In some federal states, sexuality education is integrated into broader subjects, such as biology, ethics, religion and social sciences, while in others, it is taught as a stand-alone subject. The Special Rapporteur encourages the Government to ensure that children receive age-appropriate sexuality education to equip them with the knowledge, skills, attitudes and values that help them to protect their health, develop respectful and healthy social and sexual relationships and make responsible choices, thereby reducing incidences of sexual exploitation and abuse both online and offline. 35. The Special Rapporteur was informed of the “Education in the Digital World” strategy (2016), established by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, which stipulates the promotion of digital skills among children and young people in schools and addresses such issues as critical thinking and risks in the digital environment. The Special Rapporteur’s discussions, however, revealed that there was no mandatory subject on digital literacy for children in German schools. She also learned that teachers and parents often did not have the confidence to adequately support children in cases of harm in the digital environment. The Government is urged to incorporate digital literacy for all children as a compulsory subject in all schools across the country. 36. During her visit, the Special Rapporteur learned about a creative initiative for the prevention of child sexual abuse called “Trau dich!”(Dare to do!), launched in 2013 by the Federal Ministry for Family Affairs, Senior Citizens, Women and Youth and the Federal Institute of Public Health. The initiative is aimed at empowering children from 8 to 12 years through theatrical performances that teach them about their rights and personal boundaries. The initiative includes guidance for children on where to seek help and support in cases of sexual abuse, including by facilitating the connection of schools with counselling centres and other relevant regional networks, and awareness-raising activities for schools, educators and parents, including discussion evenings and other meetings in advance of the performances. 37. The Special Rapporteur also learned about the “Schools against Sexual Violence” initiative, launched in 2016 by the Independent Federal Commissioner against Child Sexual Abuse in collaboration with education authorities of the federal states. The initiative included the development of a platform to provide schools with guidance on how to develop and implement strategies to protect children from sexual violence and the provision of information on state-specific programmes and regulations. In 2023, the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs adopted guidelines on child protection in schools, applicable to all schools in Germany. The guidelines cover the development and practical implementation of institutional safeguarding policies, called Schutzkonzepte, and measures against sexual violence in schools. During her visit, the Special Rapporteur received information that at least half of the 16 federal states had adopted or planned to adopt a law requiring schools to introduce institutional safeguarding policies as a specific child protection measure. The initiatives are laudable and should be supported, including through the strengthening of school capacity. 38. The Special Rapporteur notes with appreciation the laws mandating preventive measures to protect children in alternative care arrangements. In order to obtain a permit to operate, institutions that provide care for children must develop a strategy for protection against violence aimed at safeguarding the rights and well-being of children and must put in place appropriate procedures for reporting and child participation. The institutions must also employ staff who possess relevant qualifications and do not have criminal records. They are also mandated to regularly review staff records. For children in foster care, it is mandatory that the state-level youth welfare office develop a protection strategy, together with the caregiver and the child, to safeguard the child’s rights and to protect the child from violence throughout the duration of foster care. The youth welfare office is also required to ensure that the child knows where and how to lodge complaints. 39. The Special Rapporteur observed many campaigns throughout Germany on issues relating to child sexual abuse and exploitation. One example was Schieb deine Verantwortung nicht weg!(Don’t push away your responsibility!), launched in 2022 by the Federal Ministry for Family Affairs, Senior Citizens, Women and Youth together with the Independent Federal Commissioner against Child Sexual Abuse. The campaign highlights the collective responsibility to prevent children from becoming victims of sexual violence, calling on people from all walks of life to look more closely, listen more carefully and take action when they have any suspicion. The campaign messages are disseminated through television channels, posters, social media platforms and a wide range of information materials. Other government and law enforcement agencies have developed similar campaigns. While such efforts positively indicate the focus and efforts dedicated to preventive measures, the Special Rapporteur encourages the development of a standardized approach and the coordination of activities among child protection actors in order to harmonize the roll-out and implementation of such awareness-raising campaigns across the country. 40. With regard to the sexual exploitation of children in travel and tourism, the Special Rapporteur wishes to emphasize the need for the Government to strongly encourage commercial travel providers to subscribe to the Code of Conduct for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation in Travel and Tourism, a multi-stakeholder initiative aimed at awareness-raising within and the provision of tools and support to the tourism industry to prevent the sexual exploitation of children. Companies that adopt the code gain access to tools and resources to use in their daily operations that contribute to keeping children safe.

records.text: 32. Germany has developed strategic plans on specific aspects of child protection. In 2011, the Federal Ministry for Family Affairs, Senior Citizens, Women and Youth issued the Action Plan for the Protection of Children and Young People from Sexual Violence and Exploitation. The Action Plan is focused on prevention, support for child victims of sexual violence, the protection of children against sexual exploitation and abuse in the digital environment and in the context of tourism, protection from child trafficking for the purpose of sexual exploitation and the strengthening of research and international cooperation. While the Special Rapporteur commends the initiative, she recommends an evaluation of the Action Plan to track progress and identify gaps. 33. In 2020, the Federal Ministry for Family Affairs, Senior Citizens, Women and Youth issued a federal cooperation concept on protection and help in cases of trafficking in and exploitation of children, which contains a framework for cooperation among youth welfare offices, the police, specialized counselling centres and other entities involved in the identification and protection of child victims of trafficking in persons. Each federal state is to adapt the provisions and structures for its specific context. The Special Rapporteur welcomes the focus on children and the objective for relevant child protection actors to work together in a coordinated manner. The Special Rapporteur understands that a draft national action plan to prevent and combat trafficking in persons and protect trafficked persons is currently in development.

records.text: 26. The Office of the Independent Federal Commissioner against Child Sexual Abuse, which was established in 2010, plays a central role in protecting children from sexual exploitation and abuse, both online and offline. The Office serves as a point of contact for survivors, promotes public and political awareness of the issue, supports the development of preventive and intervention measures and supports and co-designs relevant legislation. For example, it was involved in the reform of relevant laws relating to sexual offences and social compensation and in the child-friendly reform of the Code of Criminal Procedure and of the Act on Proceedings in Family Matters and in Matters of Non-contentious Jurisdiction, which governs family law. 27. The Office of the Independent Federal Commissioner is part of a triad, together with the Survivors’ Board and the Independent Federal Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse. The Survivors’ Board comprises individuals who have personally experienced sexual abuse in childhood or adolescence to ensure that survivors’ voices and perspectives inform the work of the Independent Federal Commissioner. They bring the concerns of the survivors of sexual violence into political discourse and make the general public aware of them. The Independent Federal Inquiry investigates sexual violence against children and adolescents in both institutional and family contexts, conducting hearings involving survivors and eyewitnesses. Since its establishment in 2016, more than 2,000 confidential hearings have been held. Drawing lessons from survivors and eyewitnesses, it also prepares reports and recommendations on how to prevent sexual violence against children and adolescents and on steps that the Government and society could take to recognize the suffering experienced by survivors. 28. The Special Rapporteur notes that the National Council against Sexual Violence Committed against Children and Young People was established in 2019. It comprises 300 members from politics, civil society, academia and professional practice as well as members of the Survivors’ Board. The Council serves as a platform for interdisciplinary dialogue to foster strong cooperation at all levels. It has, for instance, provided support to the federal states in developing state-level institutions, such as survivors’ boards and inquiry commissions. 29. In 2022, the National Rapporteur Mechanism on trafficking in persons was established within the German Institute for Human Rights with the core tasks of heightening the visibility of trafficking in persons, establishing a solid base of data and monitoring case law and legislation to report on the implementation of the relevant regional and international instruments. 30. There are over 570 youth welfare offices across Germany to support parents and legal guardians in raising and caring for children. A fundamental area of responsibility of the youth welfare offices is child protection. If a child is neglected or abused, the local youth welfare office is mandated to investigate and to care for the child. In cases of urgent danger affecting a child, the office can arrange for emergency placements. The resources and capacities of youth welfare offices vary between municipalities, resulting in a shortage of personnel in some of them. It has been reported, for instance, that the ratio of child protection investigations per case worker has been steadily increasing. Echoing the recommendation of the Committee on the Rights of the Child, the Special Rapporteur encourages the Government to provide the youth welfare offices across the country with adequate resources to make their services available to all children everywhere in Germany, especially those in vulnerable situations. 31. Regarding online child sexual abuse and exploitation, the Federal Agency for Child and Youth Protection in the Media ensures joint responsibility among the State, the private sector and civil society organizations for the protection of children and young people through, among other activities, reviewing and maintaining an index of media harmful to children, ensuring the compliance of relevant service providers with their obligations under the Digital Services Act and raising public awareness of the risks posed by the media to children and young people. The Special Rapporteur was pleased to learn about the establishment in 2024 of the Federal Office for the Enforcement of Children’s Rights in Digital Services, which is responsible for supervising compliance by digital service providers with their obligations with respect to child protection. Among those are the requirements to establish structural preventive measures within their services that ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security for children, including age verification systems, parental support tools and effective reporting and remediation systems, to label their content with age ratings and to explain their terms and conditions in a child-friendly manner.

records.text: 19. In Germany, there are laws at the national, federal state and municipal levels relating to child protection. At the national level, Book VIII of the Social Code (1991) regulates the mandate, services and responsibilities of child and youth welfare services, including emergency placement, participation in family court proceedings, guardianship and approval for residential care facilities and foster families. The Social Code also stipulates that, in order to obtain a permit to operate, institutions working with children and young people must put in place policies and measures to protect them from all forms of violence, including reporting mechanisms, and to ensure the exclusion of persons with criminal records from working with children and young people. 20. The German Criminal Code (1872) criminalizes the sexual abuse of children. The Special Rapporteur notes, however, that the Criminal Code lacks specific provisions that directly address the unique and evolving nature of technology. She also notes that provisions in the Criminal Code still use such terminology as “child pornography”. There is a need to move away from such terminology as it retraumatizes and revictimizes those who have experienced abuse. She strongly urges the Government to consider reviewing any law using such terminology and to replace all references to “child pornography” with “child sexual abuse material”, in line with the Terminology Guidelines for the Protection of Children from Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse. The Criminal Code was amended in 2016 to implement the European Union Directive on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and protecting its victims, thereby including provisions for the different manifestations of trafficking, including forced prostitution, forced labour, labour exploitation, forced begging, forced criminality and organ harvesting. 21. The Special Rapporteur was pleased to learn that the German Code of Criminal Procedure (1877) provides for rules on the audiovisual recording of witness examinations in the investigation phase to avoid multiple interrogations of child victims of crimes, including sexual violence. It allows witness examination in court hearings to be done via audiovisual tools in instances where there may be an imminent risk of serious harm to the well-being of the witness. Particularly for witnesses under 18 years of age, the examination may be substituted with an audio recording of their previous judicial examination. The law also guarantees the child victim’s right to psychosocial support during court proceedings. 22. The Act on Proceedings in Family Matters and in Matters of Non-contentious Jurisdiction of 2009 contains provisions on proceedings in child protection cases. It sets priorities for certain proceedings involving children, such as child endangerment cases where an initial court hearing must be conducted within one month. In such cases, the child must be heard in person by the court, regardless of their age, so that the court can form a direct impression. In addition, a guardian ad litem must be appointed to represent the child’s interests in the proceedings. The Act on Cooperation and Information in Child Protection of 2012 mandates child and youth welfare authorities to organize a network on child protection with different institutions. It also authorizes health professionals, therapists, teachers, and other groups of professionals working with children to report cases to child and youth welfare authorities where they have reasonable grounds to suspect child endangerment, even if the children’s parents are not willing to seek support. 23. To prevent the risk of adverse impacts of business activity on human rights, including those of children, the Act on Corporate Due Diligence Obligations in Supply Chains of 2023 mandates companies to ensure human rights compliance among their entire supply chain and sets up a grievance mechanism and a requirement to report on their activities. From her discussions, however, the Special Rapporteur understands that the law applies only to large companies, those with 1,000 employees or more, which means that many companies, including commercial travel operators, whose activity may facilitate the sexual exploitation of children in the context of travel and tourism, are not subject to the law. In addition, the Digital Services Act, which became operative in 2024, applies to digital service providers operating in the member States of the European Union, including platforms, hosting services and online intermediaries, and regulates transparency obligations, content moderation, risk management and complaint and redress mechanisms for users. 24. The Social Compensation Act, which is regulated under Book XIV of the Social Code and came into force in January 2024, provides access to eligible victims of violence, including sexual abuse and exploitation, to support and assistance, including psychosocial and trauma counselling, medical treatment and financial compensation. The Special Rapporteur was pleased to learn that foreigners, irrespective of their residence status, also had access to compensation. She looks forward to learning about the implementation of the law and its impact on the response to the needs of child victims of sexual abuse and sexual exploitation. 25. During the Special Rapporteur’s visit, she learned that a draft act to strengthen structures against sexual violence against children and young people was under discussion in the Parliament, with the key goals of institutionalizing the Independent Federal Commissioner against Child Sexual Abuse, the Survivors’ Board and the Independent Federal Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse and establishing a reporting obligation for the Federal Commissioner and the Federal Inquiry to regularly report on the extent of child sexual abuse and the current status of protection, assistance, research and investigation in Germany. The Special Rapporteur commends the Government for the significant steps it has taken to reinforce the country’s commitment to child protection, ensuring that child sexual abuse is met with a comprehensive, coordinated and child-centred approach.

records.text: 15. Germany has ratified major international human rights instruments, including eight of the nine core international human rights instruments of the United Nations. 16. Germany ratified the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1992, the Optional Protocol on the involvement of children in armed conflict in 2004, the Optional Protocol on the sale of children, child prostitution and child pornography in 2009 and the Optional Protocol on a communications procedure in 2013. 17. Germany is also a Party to the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime and the Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, Especially Women and Children, supplementing the Organized Crime Convention, the Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, the Convention on Jurisdiction, Applicable Law, Recognition, Enforcement and Cooperation in Respect of Parental Responsibility and Measures for the Protection of Children, the Convention on Protection of Children and Cooperation in respect of Intercountry Adoption and the Forced Labour Convention, 1930 (No. 29), the Abolition of Forced Labour Convention, 1957 (No. 105), and the Worst Forms of Child Labour Convention, 1999 (No. 182), of the International Labour Organization. 18. At the regional level, Germany is bound by the following Council of Europe conventions: the Convention on the Protection of Children against Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse; the Convention on Cybercrime; the Convention on Preventing and Combating Violence against Women and Domestic Violence; and the Convention on Action against Trafficking in Human Beings. It is also bound by European Union directives 2011/36/EU on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and protecting its victims, and replacing Council Framework Decision 2002/629/JHA, as well as its amendments, and 2011/93/EU on combating the sexual abuse and sexual exploitation of children and child pornography. The Special Rapporteur understands that there is currently a proposal to recast the latter directive. The proposal includes an expansion of the definition of offences relating to child sexual abuse in the light of new technological developments, the extension of the time limit for prosecution and the replacement of all references to “child pornography” with “child sexual abuse material” among other changes. That would be a major step towards reflecting the realities of technological developments and the emerging risks in child sexual abuse and exploitation. She encourages the Government to support the proposal.

records.text: 14. The Special Rapporteur’s discussions with interlocutors revealed that many of the victims of child trafficking for the purpose of sexual exploitation in Germany fell within the age range of 15–17 years and came from Bulgaria, Czechia, Poland and Romania. They were often boys who had grown up in poverty and had been forced into sex work to support their families back home. They often lacked identification documents, a registered address and health insurance. She learned, however, that various stakeholders, including civil society organizations, the police and communities, worked in close cooperation to organize public awareness-raising campaigns in affected neighbourhoods and to provide care, counselling and support services. The Special Rapporteur urges that more be done to address the root causes of the problem, including cooperation with the countries of origin of such children.

records.text: 13. Refugee and asylum-seeking children in Germany face a higher risk of falling victim to sexual abuse and trafficking. Language barriers and the children’s living conditions and lack of knowledge about German systems and support services exacerbate their vulnerability. Systemic protection strategies against violence in reception and collective accommodation facilities are necessary to protect residents from recruitment by traffickers. The Special Rapporteur is pleased to note that the Federal Ministry for Family Affairs, Senior Citizens, Women and Youth and UNICEF, together with many partner organizations within the Protection of Refugees in Refugee Accommodation initiative, have developed the Minimum Standards for the Protection of Refugees in Refugee Accommodation Centres, which contain a differentiated focus on children and young people as a group in particular need of protection. The guidance also provides specific recommendations for protection, participation and access to services for LGBTQI+ refugees, refugees with disabilities and refugees with trauma-related disorders.

records.text: 12. In Germany, as elsewhere, children with disabilities are at heightened risk of becoming victims of sexual abuse and exploitation. Relationships of dependency can quickly develop in contexts where there is intensive contact between children and adults, such as in childcare, education, counselling or therapy, and within the family. Perpetrators may exploit such dependency along with other particular circumstances of children with disabilities, such as social isolation and limited communication or mobility. They may cross the line between care and sexually motivated assault in a way that is not apparent to other people.

records.section: Online child sexual exploitation and abuse and child sexual abuse material
records.text: 11. The digital environment has been playing an increasingly important role in cases of sexual abuse and exploitation of children. In Germany, according to the Federal Criminal Police Office, the number of cases of production, distribution, acquisition and possessionof child sexual abuse materialhas risen steadily in recent years, reaching 45,191 cases in 2023, three times the number in 2019, in which 12,262 cases were recorded. In her discussions in the country, the Special Rapporteur learned about an increasing trend of live-streaming child sexual abuse, with perpetrators residing in Germany facilitating and instructing others in the sexual abuse of children abroad. She learned that, in many cases, the perpetrators had provided such precise and horrific instructions that it was as if they themselves had directly abused the children. The same increasing trend has been found in “cybergrooming”, where perpetrators establish contact with potential child victims in chat rooms and social networks, “sharenting”, where parents share publicly the day-to-day lives of their children, “kidfluencing”, where children gain significant followings on social media platforms by creating content that appeals to young audiences, and sextortion, where perpetrators use a child’s sexual images or videos to blackmail or extort them for money or more sexually explicit materials. The Special Rapporteur also learned that criminals in Germany were increasingly abusing everyday images of children for sexual purposes. Such images were available on both the clearnet and darknet, and criminals placed hundreds of thousands of sexualizing comments underneath.

records.section: Sexual exploitation of children in the context of travel and tourism
records.text: 10. In Germany, commercial travel operators offer a mixture of voluntary service and tourism, known as voluntourism. A survey conducted in September 2023 with 25 commercial travel providers that targeted the German market found that all of them provided offers for volunteering abroad and that the demand for voluntourism continued to increase. Projects with children were the most popular area for volunteering. Nine of the surveyed travel providers offered placements in orphanages. Voluntourism may expose children to risks to their safety, well-being and development, including sexual abuse and exploitation, especially without adequate safeguards and preventive measures in place. The survey revealed that fewer than half of the travel providers had codes of conduct for their volunteers that included child protection guidelines or required the volunteers to submit criminal records.

records.section: Trafficking in children for the purpose of sexual exploitation
records.text: 9. In Germany, commercial sexual exploitation appears to be the most prevalent form of trafficking in children. In 2023, according to the Federal Criminal Police Office, there were 182 cases of child sexual exploitation, with 216 child victims identified; 74.2 per cent were female. Of the child victims, 78.6 per cent were nationals of Germany, while the non‐German victims were most commonly nationals of Romania and the Syrian Arab Republic. The methods through which children are brought into situations of exploitation in Germany vary greatly and range from exploitation by family members to organized structures of violence. Sometimes the identity documents of children of foreign nationalities are taken away from them. Some do not speak German and may not know the law and their rights. Some may be fearful of the authorities. In some cases, the children are a source of income for their family in their country of origin. While some are in Germany with their parents or guardians, others are unaccompanied. Children who have been trafficked and exploited are often subject to various conflicts of loyalty, where breaking out of the situation can seem like a betrayal of their family or their community.

records.section: Sexual abuse of minors within communities and the circle of trust
records.text: 8. In 2023, according to the Federal Criminal Police Office, there were 16,375 cases of sexual abuse of children, a 5.5 per cent increase over 2022. Of the 18,497 child victims recorded, 75.6 per cent were female and 24.4 per cent were male; 15,460 victims were German, while 3,037 were nationals of other countries, the majority from Romania, the Syrian Arab Republic and Ukraine. In most cases, there was an established relationship between the victims and the perpetrators, who included family members, friends and acquaintances, or a formal social relationship stemming from an institution, organization or group, such as a sports club or religious institution. In the context of religious institutions, interlocutors reported that there had been a lack of accountability and transparency regarding data on child sexual abuse and the compensation paid to victims.

records.text: 4. Germany is a federation comprising 16 federal states (Länder). Each of the federal states has its own constitution, parliament, administrative structures and responsibilities. The exercise of state powers and the discharge of state functions are generally the responsibility of the federal states. Local authorities (municipalities and associations of municipalities) are part of the federal states, with the constitutionally guaranteed right to regulate all local affairs under their own responsibility, within the limits prescribed by law. 5. In 2023, the population of Germany was 84,669,326, with children (under 18 years) accounting for 14,303,363 of the total. Foreigners made up 13,895,865 of the population. Over 36 per cent of the foreigners were nationals of European Union countries; the top five countries represented were Bulgaria, Croatia, Italy, Poland and Romania. The remaining 63 per cent were nationals of non-European Union countries, the majority from Afghanistan, the Russian Federation, the Syrian Arab Republic, Türkiye and Ukraine. Germany saw a sharp rise in the number of people arriving from conflict and crisis zones, especially in 2015, 2016 and 2022. As of 2023, 2,983,464 people were under the mandate of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Germany, including refugees, asylum-seekers and stateless persons. The majority were from Afghanistan, the Syrian Arab Republic and Ukraine, with children making up 28.5 per cent. 6. In line with its Basic Law, Germany acknowledges inviolable and inalienable human rights as the basis of every community and of peace and justice in the world. Human rights are a key pillar of the work of the Government, which continuously strives to strengthen civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights in the country. Some of its priorities are the human rights of women and girls, children and adolescents, persons with disabilities, older persons and refugees and migrants, as well as combating climate change and racism. 7. The Basic Law affirms that the care and upbringing of children are the right and duty of parents. Although it does not mention children’s rights, children are entitled to all the fundamental rights enshrined within it. According to the case law of the Federal Constitutional Court, children have a right to protection and assistance to develop into self‐reliant persons in society. Most of the federal state constitutions include references to children’s rights.

records.text: The Special Rapporteur recommends that the Government of Germany: (a) Repatriate, as a matter of utmost urgency, all its citizens and individuals who have close ties with it who are still detained in the north-east of the Syrian Arab Republic. Special attention should be paid to minors and their mothers, and the boys and men in prisons; (b) Engage with all relevant parties in the north-east of the Syrian Arab Republic to ascertain the precise whereabouts of its detained citizens and those who have close ties with the country, as well as the current state of their health and welfare. Particular attention should be paid to those individuals who have contracted tuberculosis or other life-threatening illnesses, as well as identifying nationals who have died in prisons; (c) Fully engage and support families of individuals detained in the north-east of the Syrian Arab Republic and communicate with families and update them on the status and whereabouts of those detained, particularly if there have been deaths or illnesses in custody; (d) Continue to pursue accountability for victims of terrorism through the innovative, courageous and groundbreaking use of national criminal law, in accordance with international human rights law, to ensure accountability for core crimes committed in conflict zones; (e) Continue to uphold international fair trial standards in cases involving cumulative charging, including due care in relation to the use of plea bargains, witness evidence, “ battlefield evidence ” and new criteria for criminal liability. The Special Rapporteur recommends a particularly cautious approach to the use of gendered criteria, such as marriage, as the basis for any criminal liability; (f) Adequately fund NGOs carrying out critical reintegration work in the medium or long term, refrain from creating a hostile environment for such NGOs through surveillance or prosecution of civil society actors working on reintegration and consistently validate the work of civil society; (g) Treat with dignity individuals who have served their sentences in relation to travel to conflict zones, association or core crimes. Support for their full reintegration into German society should be provided, including continuing meaningful contact and early reunion with their family, including children; (h) Proactively share knowledge and experiences of both reintegration and prosecution strategies developed by Germany with other States.

records.text: 62. The Special Rapporteur recognizes the positive work of the Governments of Germany and North Macedonia in making substantial efforts to repatriate a significant number of their nationals from the conflict zone of the north-east of the Syrian Arab Republic. She affirms the life-changing consequences for both German and Macedonian children, as a result of the ruinous and dignity-denying realities of arbitrary and tortuous conditions in camps and prisons and the transformative possibilities that are facilitated by returning to the country of nationality. The return of children is an integral part of a State party’s obligations under the Convention on the Rights of the Child. It affirms the potential of the children and armed conflict agenda through meaningful practice and practical implementation. The Special Rapporteur particularly commends the Government of North Macedonia for its positive practice of returning men from prison facilities in the north-east of the Syrian Arab Republic. She positively supports the efforts of both Governments to facilitate positive repatriation, based on a fundamental commitment to reintegrate individuals back into society and demonstrate faith in individuals’ capacity to transform their lives and positively engage in society. She acknowledges the unique efforts of Germany to support the human rights of victims of terrorism, pursue justice for the most serious international crimes and fill the evidence lacunae for violations of human rights and humanitarian law that have followed the conflict in the north-east of the Syrian Arab Republic. 63. Given the positive practice demonstrated in both States, as well as innovative solutions developed for community integration, prosecution, and preventing and countering violent extremism, the Special Rapporteur urges both States to be leaders in the ongoing work of returning all their nationals from conflict zones, including men, women and, particularly, children. She urges all relevant Governments to facilitate the return of all of their nationals, men, women and children, from a situation of detention in which core international crimes are being committed through indefinite arbitrary detention, incommunicado detention, disappearances, torture, enforced separation, sexual violence, starvation and the denial of necessary medical treatment. 64. Given the evidence of positive practice witnessed during the joint visit, the Special Rapporteur urges other States whose nationals (men, women and children) remain detained in the north-east of the Syrian Arab Republic to live up to their international human rights and international humanitarian law obligations, to actively pursue return and repatriation in cooperation with all relevant actors, to seek innovative interdisciplinary and community-based approaches to reintegration, to pursue international criminal justice (in accordance with international law) and to no longer tolerate systematic human rights violations committed with impunity against their civilians held in mass arbitrary detention in the north-east of the Syrian Arab Republic.

In addressing discrimination, the authorities should: (a) Take specific and special measures at all levels, and with the meaningful participation of groups and communities involved, for reducing discrimination, including indirect, structural and intersectional measures, and address the widespread and continuing stereotyping and marginalization of specific sections of the population; (b) Strengthen the monitoring and reporting of the right not to be discriminated against in cultural activities, including in reporting to the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination; (c) Review their application of minority protection to fully conform with the guidance of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, as contained in Protecting Minority Rights: A Practical Guide to Developing Comprehensive Anti-Discrimination Legislation; (d) Ratify the International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families and the Marrakesh Treaty to Facilitate Access to Published Works for Persons Who Are Blind, Visually Impaired, or Otherwise Print Disabled, in order to facilitate the full participation of the persons concerned in all aspects of cultural life; (e) Consider adopting guidelines for applying the Equal Treatment Act also to private actors, in particular regarding access to, and participation in the activities of, cultural venues; (f) Take steps to ensure that reasonable accommodation provisions are enshrined in law as an immediately enforceable right in all areas of law and policy. Authorities should also take positive measures in the implementation of the Equal Treatment Act, ensuring that the denial of reasonable accommodation is recognized as a form of discrimination and punished accordingly; (g) Ensure that teaching materials that promote diversity and the protection of all minority groups are available across all federal states, and include in national teacher training programmes a module on respect for diversity in education. This content should be protected as a fundamental element of educational systems, and maintained despite any political pressure; (h) Support projects that reduce discrimination against LGBTIQ+ persons, and work for the protection and recognition of sexual diversity; (i) Introduce incentives to the media to promote positive images of minorities, migrants, refugees and asylum-seeking persons, including women and LGBTIQ+ persons.

To improve the understanding and full realization of cultural rights, the Government should: (a) Incorporate all international human rights instruments, including the Optional Protocol to the Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, into its legal system in ways that ensure their direct application before German courts, in order to afford all individuals its full protection; (b) Disseminate and enable discussion of the provisions of international human rights law relating to cultural rights and of the present report, at the national, state and local levels, in particular among parliamentarians, public officials and judicial authorities, in order to improve awareness of the cultural rights standards and obligations contracted by Germany and their full implementation at all levels; (c) Include explicit references to cultural rights in the federal, state or local laws, programmes and regulations, and in particular, in the Participation Act; (d) Raise awareness, through campaigns in educational institutions, the public arena and the media, of the definition of cultural rights, including the right for all to take part in cultural life, to express one’s own identity, values and way of life without fear of discrimination, and to access and enjoy the arts, science and sports; (e) Establish minimum standards and guidelines for reducing disparities and ensuring that all people, regardless of their place of residence, can fully enjoy and exercise their cultural rights, and closely monitor the implementation of those rights at all levels; (f) Include international human rights instruments in the curricula of universities and legal studies; (g) Conduct regular and mandatory training on intercultural competencies across all ministries and local authorities, as well as for education professionals and members of the police force, and ensure that the training includes the standards and norms of both human rights and cultural rights.

records.text: 88. Germany has made significant progress in recognizing its difficult past and the changes in its society, and in building a sophisticated legal and policy framework to uphold its international human rights and humanitarian law commitments. 89. There needs to be better understanding and coordination of cultural rights within the multi-layered administration of Germany, and clearer leadership from the Federal Government in ensuring the full implementation of those rights. International standards should be considered in national discussions regarding cultural matters and more discussion among different public bodies on such matters needs to be encouraged. International human rights standards on non-discrimination and participation, including cultural participation and the effective participation of minorities, should guide any relevant new legislation and be considered in all public policies. This would increase the visibility and understanding of these rights, help raise awareness for the standards and obligations and ensure that all relevant public institutions and bodies play their role in meeting the country’s existing obligations. 90. The Special Rapporteur admires the vibrancy and engagement of German civil society and of the cultural sector towards cultural diversity, as well as the numerous associated excellent practices, and welcomes the commitments and legislation recently adopted to better respect and protect that diversity. 91. In addressing the challenges of multicultural realities, German authorities should, however, make better use of the international human rights standards and guidance on cultural rights, and ensure that they are better disseminated, known and implemented at all levels of the country’s federal system. The voluntary, ad hoc and temporary initiatives for implementing cultural rights remain fragile for as long as they are not structurally anchored in long-term strategies and policies.

records.section: Preparation of the next periodic report
records.text: 59. The Committee recommends that the State party submit its combined twenty ‐ seventh to twenty-ninth periodic reports, as a single document, by 15 June 2027, taking into account the reporting guidelines adopted by the Committee during its seventy-first session and addressing all the points raised in the present concluding observations. In the light of General Assembly resolution 68/268, the Committee urges the State party to observe the limit of 21,200 words for periodic reports.
themes: Cooperation & Follow up with Treaty Bodies

records.text: 58. The Committee wishes to draw the attention of the State party to the particular importance of the recommendations contained in paragraph 16 (racist hate speech and crimes), paragraph 18 (racial profiling and use of force by enforcement officials), paragraph 24 (right to education) and paragraph 46 (reparation for colonial past) above and requests the State party to provide detailed information in its next periodic report on the concrete measures taken to implement those recommendations.

records.section: Follow-up to the present concluding observations
records.text: 57. In accordance with article 9 (1) of the Convention and rule 65 of its rules of procedure, the Committee requests the State party to provide, within one year of the adoption of the present concluding observations, information on its implementation of the recommendations contained in paragraphs 14 (a), (b) and (c) (General Equal Treatment Act) and paragraphs 38 (b) and (c) (Discrimination against non-citizens) above.
themes: Cooperation & Follow up with Treaty Bodies

records.text: 56. The Committee encourages the State party to update its common core document, which dates to 8 November 2016, in accordance with the harmonized guidelines on reporting under the international human rights treaties, in particular those on the common core document, as adopted at the fifth inter-committee meeting of the human rights treaty bodies held in June 2006. In the light of General Assembly resolution 68/268, the Committee urges the State party to observe the limit of 42,400 words for such documents.
themes: Cooperation & Follow up with Treaty Bodies

records.text: 55. The Committee recommends that the State party’s reports be made readily available and accessible to the public at the time of their submission and that the concluding observations of the Committee with respect to those reports be similarly made available to all State bodies entrusted with the implementation of the Convention, including all federal states and municipalities, and publicized on the website of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in the official and other commonly used languages, as appropriate.
themes: Cooperation & Follow up with Treaty Bodies
Human rights education, trainings & awareness raising

records.text: 54. The Committee recommends that the State party continue consulting and increasing its dialogue with civil society organizations working in the area of human rights protection, in particular those working to combat racial discrimination, in connection with the preparation of its next periodic report and in follow-up to the present concluding observations.

records.section: International Decade for People of African Descent
records.text: 53. In the light of General Assembly resolution 68/237, in which the Assembly proclaimed 2015–2024 the International Decade for People of African Descent, and Assembly resolution 69/16 on the programme of activities for the implementation of the Decade, the Committee recommends that the State party prepare and implement a suitable programme of measures and policies in collaboration with organizations and peoples of African descent. The Committee requests that the State party include in its next report precise information on concrete measures adopted in that framework, taking into account its general recommendation No. 34 (2011) on racial discrimination against people of African descent.

records.section: Follow-up to the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action
records.text: 52. In the light of its general recommendation No. 33 (2009) on follow-up to the Durban Review Conference, the Committee recommends that , when implementing the Convention in its domestic legal order, the State party give effect to the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, adopted in September 2001 at the World Conference against Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance, taking into account the outcome document of the Durban Review Conference, held in Geneva in April 2009 . The Committee requests that the State party include in its next periodic report specific information on action plans and other measures taken to implement the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action at the national level.

records.text: 47. The Committee welcomes the recognition by the Government of Germany of its wrongful colonial acts and acknowledges the apologies expressed for the genocide of the Ovaherero and Nama peoples in Namibia, including the joint declaration by the German and Namibian Governments in May 2021 and the recent apology by the President of Germany for colonial wrongdoings in the United Republic of Tanzania. The Committee also welcomes the measures for the restitution of colonial items. While noting that colonial experiences may differ from one and other, the Committee is concerned about the lack of: (a) A more comprehensive approach towards reparation for colonial wrongdoings in terms of restitution, compensation and satisfaction, as appropriate; (b) Meaningful participation of the representatives of the victims of the Ovaherero and Nama people’s genocide in the development and adoption of the joint declaration; (c) A comprehensive policy for the restitution of colonial objects and cultural artifacts, in particular the restitution of the human remains of ancestors (art. 6).
